title: The 9 key climbs of the Vuelta a España 2026
content:
Cyclist
The 9 key climbs of the Vuelta a España 2026

The Vuelta a España packs in approximately 58,000m of elevation gain for the 2026 edition, a slight increase over the 2025 race won by Jonas Vingegaard. The race kicks off in Monaco and travels to Andorra before dipping into the Pyrenees early and brings seven summit finishes and even some gravel to spice things up.

Here we look at the key climbs that should play a part in shaking up the final podium in Granada on 13th September.

Stage 4: Port d’Envalira (23.2km, 4.9%)

No one can afford to ride into their best form in this year’s Vuelta. Stage 4 takes the peloton around a location many pro cyclists will be familiar with in Andorra. Climbing begins from the flag drop with the day’s first ascent of the Port d’Envalira. At 23.2km, it’s the longest ascent of the race and delivers a rollercoaster of 7% lumps towards the long road to the summit.

Recovery on the day isn’t too much of an option either as it’s followed by the Collada de Beixalis (6.5km, 8.5%), which hits almost 13% at its peak just over a kilometre into scaling it, and the Coll d’Ordino which is almost 10km and is one constant slog of 7% with no easier a gradient to be found.

Stage 6: Puerto El Bartolo (9.4km, 7%)

Ah, gravel. Love it or hate it, there’s seemingly no escaping it in recent Grand Tours. The Vuelta has tended to steer clear of it more than the Giro or Tour, its last notable inclusion in Spain coming back in 2019 on a day that saw Tadej Pogačar claim his first Grand Tour stage win and Primož Roglič crash.

The Puerto El Bartolo is making its debut in the race and packs a big punch. As well as dealing with unpaved roads, riders must contend with double-figure gradients over halfway into the climb as a slight 500m of respite tees up the final 500m slog of 8% to the top.

Stage 7: Aramón Valdelinares (9.8km, 5.9%)

Stage 7 is a day trending consistently uphill in the final 50km, packing in three climbs with the Category 2 Puetro de San Rafael (11.2km, 4.4%) signalling the final test is on the horizon.

Aramón Valdelinares clocks 9% at its peak and while it’s not the hardest of climbs to deal with, it is the race’s first serious summit finish. Winner Anacona lived up to his name with victory here in 2014.

Stage 9: Alto de Aitana (21.9km, 5.8%)

Now we’re talking. The Alto de Aitana is the second longest climb of this year’s Vuelta at 21.9km, remaining steady at around 5% for the opening half and ramping up to 9.3% at its peak 17km into the climb, the final 3km averaging about 7% towards the line.

It last reared its head back in 2016 on the penultimate stage of the race, where AG2R-La Mondiale’s Pierre Latour won ahead of Darwin Atapuma of BMC Racing Team. This year the stage is situated just prior to the first rest day.

Stage 12: Calar Alto (17km, 5.6%)

The finish location for Stage 12 is Calar Alto, the second half of a 1-2 punch that follows the Alto de Velefique (13.1km, 7.2%) just north of Almería and the location of the largest astronomical observatory in Europe. The climb begins harshly, introducing double-figure gradients after just 2km uphill, then flattens out only to rocket back up to 10% at the 14km point. It settles back down and flitters between 2-4%, then smacks a short and steep finish of 7% in the final 200m.

This climbing duo was last utilised in 2017. On Stage 11 that year, Astana’s Miguel Ángel López broke away from Team Sky’s Chris Froome and Bahrain Merida’s Vincenzo Nibali to claim the victory. López has since been suspended until 2027, Froome recently quietly retired and Nibali stepped off the bike in 2022.

Stage 14: Sierra de la Pandera (11.8km, 7.5%)

Vuelta race director Fernando Escartín notes that the Sierra de la Panderra finish, combined with the potential of high temperatures, means a rider having a bad day ‘can kiss the general classification goodbye’.

The first 130-odd kilometres of the 154km day shouldn’t pose too much of a threat, with just a couple of Category 2 climbs to contend with, but the summit finish hits 13% at its peak. Both Rafal Majka and Richard Carapaz have the honour of having won atop the summit in the two most recent instalments of the Sierra de la Pandera. The year Carapaz won, 2022, he would go on to win the mountains classification, and he’s back again this year with eyes on GC.

Stage 19: Peñas Blancas (18.7km, 6.5%)

This is another climb that Richard Carapaz is familiar with, having also won atop it in 2022. The penultimate mountain stage scales three summits prior to the finishing location of Peñas Blancas.

18.7km in length and packing eight hairpin turns, it quickly delivers its max gradient of 17% to make or break anyone’s hopes of success. Whether it will be overly decisive for the podium given the day that follows is up for debate, this teetering towards last-chance saloon for any breakaway artists who want to leave their mark on the race.

Stage 20: Puerto de El Purche (8.2km, 8.1%)

The final GC day hosts over 5,000m of climbing and a double ascent of Puerto de El Purche (8.2km, 8.1%), consistently dipping into double figure gradient territory with 18% arriving close to the summit. Riders will then loop around back to the historical town of Granada – which recently suffered three earthquakes, the largest at 4.7 magnitude – to do it all over again.

The Vuelta follows both the Giro and the Tour in having included two ascents of one mountain close to the end of their races in 2026. A Piancavallo double-dipping in Italy arrived during Stage 20 and Alpe d’Huez was undertaken on Stage 19 and Stage 20 in France.

Stage 20: Collado del Alguacil (8.4km, 9.9%)

The last summit finish is a HC climb in the Collado del Alguacil, where any final decisions in terms of the Vuelta podium will be made. The 8.4km stretch crests 11% gradient immediately and brings a maximum gradient of 16% at the summit, delivering what organisers will hope to be a bang on its debut at the race.
